awd_titl_txt: WHOI/PFPE Oceanographic Instrumentation - Toward the completion of upgrading UNOLS Academic Research Fleet marine gravimetry capability
awd_abstract_narration:
The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) requests funds for oceanographic instrumentation that are needed to carry out NSF-supported scientific research on board the R/V Langseth, a research vessel operating as part of the U.S. Academic Research Fleet (ARF). The specific instrument requested is a DgS digital gravity meter to replace an older BGM-3 marine gravimeter that suffered a catastrophic failure. The new instrument will help ensure the vessel maintains its high-level capabilities to support NSF-funded research.

The principal impact of the present proposal is under Merit Review Criterion 2 of the Proposal Guidelines (NSF 23-525). It provides infrastructure support for scientists to use the vessel and its shared-use instrumentation in support of their NSF-funded oceanographic research projects (which individually undergo separate review by the relevant research program of NSF). The acquisition, maintenance, and operation of shared-use instrumentation allows NSF-funded researchers from any US university or other organization access to well-maintained, high-quality, calibrated instruments for their research. It ensures the collection of high-quality oceanographic data in support of science, reduces the cost of that research, and expands the base of potential researchers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project upgraded the United States' ability to collect high-quality gravity measurements from research vessels at sea. Marine gravity data help scientists understand the structure of the seafloor, ocean basins, and Earth's crust — knowledge that also supports national security by improving models of Earth's gravity field.


The project funded the purchase, installation, and operation of a modern Dynamic Gravity Systems AT1M marine gravimeter aboard the research vessel Marcus G. Langseth, replacing an antique BGM3 gravimeter that had become costly to maintain due to obsolete electronics, scarce spare parts, and complex shipping and calibration needs. Installation took place during a 2025 port call in San Diego, with support from the manufacturer's engineers. Vessel technicians were trained on the new system, which is now integrated into the ship's data pipeline.


The Langseth is one of the nation's primary vessels for marine seismic research and multi-science purpose operations, and gravity data provide a valuable complement — helping scientists interpret crustal structure, seafloor topography, sediment thickness, and tectonic activity. This project showed that the AT1M can deliver science-quality gravity data aboard Global- and Ocean-class research vessels, marking a key step toward completing the product life cycle of legacy BGM3 systems fleet-wide.


Because the new instrument runs continuously in the background, it collects gravity data on any cruise, even when gravity isn't the expedition's main focus. Data from eight cruises have already been submitted to the Rolling Deck to Repository (R2R) database and will become publicly available soon after each cruise or after a standard data moratorium, benefiting researchers, educators, and government agencies alike.


The project also built expertise: a WHOI postdoctoral researcher gained hands-on experience with instrument installation and data processing, marine technicians developed new instrumentation skills, and students sailing aboard the Langseth now have access to modern gravity data collection in action.
By replacing a legacy , high-maintenance system with a modern one, this project cut maintenance burdens, improved efficiency, supported open data practices, and helped preserve a nationally important scientific capability.
